what: Borrows $11.25B: $10B for affordable rental housing, supportive housing, homeownership help and farmworker/student/tribal housing, plus $1.25B for veterans' home loans.
y: The state can borrow $11.25B for these housing programs.
fiscal: About $500–600M a year for ~25 years to repay (veterans' share is repaid by borrowers).
pro: Gov. Newsom, CA Apartment Association, Habitat for Humanity, AFL-CIO
con: No organised opposition; some Republican legislators

what: Raises the cap on the state's reserve fund from 10% to 20% of general-fund taxes and extends required extra debt payments to 2040.
y: The state saves more in good years.
fiscal: Higher reserves and possibly more debt payments; no dollar estimate.
pro: Gov. Newsom, CA Professional Firefighters, LA Chamber
con: Reform California, legislative Republicans

what: Makes permanent the 10.3%, 11.3% and 12.3% state income-tax brackets on high earners (first passed in 2012), which otherwise expire after 2030.
fiscal: Keeps $5–15B a year that would otherwise disappear; about 40% to schools and community colleges.
pro: CA Teachers Association, CA State PTA, CA Medical Association, Planned Parenthood
con: CA Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association, Reform California

what: Repeals the 1988 statewide ban on public financing of campaigns, so the state and cities could create voluntary programs (not paid for from education, transport or public-safety money).
y: Governments may create public financing programs.
fiscal: A few hundred thousand dollars a year for the state ethics commission.
pro: Common Cause, League of Women Voters, ACLU
con: CA Taxpayers Association, Reform California

what: Recall ballots would only ask whether to remove the official. The seat would be filled later by special election (the lieutenant governor acts as governor meanwhile), and the recalled official could run.
y: No replacement question on recall ballots.
n: Recall and replacement on the same ballot, as now.
fiscal: Unknown; millions in savings or costs depending on the office if a recall happens.
pro: Sen. Josh Newman, Secretary of State, League of Women Voters, Common Cause
con: Election Integrity Project California, most Republican legislators

t: Loans for middle-income buyers of new homes
what: The state housing agency issues $25B of revenue bonds to lend up to 17% of the price of a newly built home (price cap ~$1.5M, income up to 200% of area median, 3% down).
fiscal: No direct state cost; homebuyers' payments repay the bonds.
pro: CA Association of Realtors, Carpenters union, Treasurer Fiona Ma
con: No organised campaign; League of Women Voters and Reform California oppose

what: Borrows $8.4B for immunology and immunotherapy research: half to a new UC-affiliated nonprofit institute, half to competitive grants. Resulting drugs offered to Californians at a 20% discount.
y: The state borrows $8.4B for this research.
fiscal: About $500–600M a year for ~20 years to repay, possibly offset by research revenue.
pro: Sponsor Gary Michelson, Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer's Association
con: Stanford's Robert Kaplan, Courage California, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn

what: Requires government ID to vote in person, and the last four digits of a government ID on mail-ballot envelopes; adds citizenship-verification reporting. Counties would issue free ID cards.
y: Extra ID information every time you vote.
n: Identity stays verified by signature matching.
fiscal: Tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year to implement.
pro: Reform California (Carl DeMaio), Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; $17M from Richard Uihlein
con: ACLU, Common Cause, League of Women Voters

what: A one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the ~200 Californians worth over $1B (residents as of 1 Jan 2026), payable over up to five years. 90% goes to health care including Medi-Cal; 10% to education and food aid.
y: The state collects the one-time tax.
fiscal: Tens of billions over several years (backers say ~$100B); possibly under $1B a year less income tax if billionaires leave.
pro: SEIU-UHW, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Teamsters, AFSCME
con: Gov. Newsom, CA Teachers Association, CA Medical Association, Planned Parenthood, SF Democratic Party; $200M+ from tech donors incl. Sergey Brin

what: Cancels any new state tax since 1 Jan 2026 that exempts its revenue from the state spending limit (i.e. Prop 40), and requires State Auditor reviews before and after new special taxes.
y: Audits required; Prop 40 is cancelled if 41 gets more votes.
fiscal: Unknown; depends on future decisions.
pro: Building a Better California (tech donors), Sergey Brin, CA Taxpayers Association
con: SEIU-UHW, Bernie Sanders

what: Constitutionally bans new state taxes on owning financial assets, business interests, art and IP, and most retroactive state taxes. Cancels conflicting taxes since 1 Jan 2026 (i.e. Prop 40). Real estate and local taxes untouched.
y: The state could never tax holdings like brokerage or stock accounts.
fiscal: Tax revenue may not grow as much in future; no dollar estimate.
pro: Building a Better California, Sergey Brin, CA Professional Firefighters, State Building Trades
con: SEIU-UHW

t: Two-thirds vote for citizen local special taxes
what: From 2027, local special taxes put on the ballot by citizen initiative would need a two-thirds vote instead of a simple majority. Future taxes only.
n: A majority can still pass them.
fiscal: Local tax revenue may grow less; size unknown.
pro: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn, CA Business Roundtable
con: SEIU, CA Democratic Party, transit advocates

t: Clinics must spend 90% on program services
what: Nonprofit community health centres (FQHCs) must spend at least 90% of revenue on program services or pay penalties, enforced by the Attorney General.
y: New spending requirement on these clinics.
fiscal: State costs in the low tens of millions a year, covered by fees.
pro: SEIU-UHW
con: CA Primary Care Association, CA Medical Association, American Academy of Pediatrics–CA, Planned Parenthood

t: Faster environmental review for essential projects
what: Time limits on CEQA review for housing, clean energy, water, health, transit, broadband and school projects: 365 days for an environmental report, 270 days for lawsuits, and courts can only halt the part that fails.
fiscal: Initial costs in the high tens of millions, possibly over $100M a year, partly covered by fees; long-term effects uncertain.
pro: CalChamber, Building Industry Assn, CA Hospital Assn, NAACP California
con: CA Labor Federation, CA Nurses Assn, Sierra Club, Western Center on Law & Poverty

what: Cuts the number of city commissions (55 to about 38 by one count), moves others out of the Charter into ordinary law, and changes how legal settlements are approved.
y: A slimmer Charter and fewer commissions.
fiscal: Saves about $365K–450K a year.
pro: Mayor Lurie, most of the Board of Supervisors
con: Coalition on Homelessness (less public oversight)

t: Municipal finance corporation and public bank
what: Authorises (doesn't require) a city lending corporation that could become a public bank with state and federal approval.
fiscal: Nothing unless the city acts; if it does, about $310–460M over 8 years. The Controller calls the uncertainty high.
pro: SF Public Bank Coalition, Labor Council, SF Democratic Party
con: SF Chronicle, SPUR, GrowSF, SF Republican Party

t: More money for the Housing Trust Fund
type: Charter amendment · by D7's Sup. Melgar
what: Raises the city's annual affordable-housing set-aside from about $50M to $125M by 2034–35, extends it to 2058, and lifts the down-payment-loan income cap to 200% of area median. Can be paused in deficit years.
fiscal: No new tax; moves up to about $60M a year of existing general-fund money by 2034–35.
pro: Housing nonprofits, SF Democratic Party, SF Chronicle, SPUR, GrowSF
con: SF Republican Party (a set-aside during a deficit)

t: Harder to put measures on the ballot
what: Ends the Mayor's and four supervisors' power to place measures directly (a Board majority needed), and raises citizen-initiative signatures from 2% to 8% of voters (about 10,600 to 42,500).
fiscal: Minimal; may save printing and special-election costs.
pro: Mayor Lurie, SF Democratic Party, SF Chronicle, SPUR, GrowSF
con: Labor Council, Tenants Union, the League, SF Republican Party

what: Gives the City Administrator sole power over contracting rules (including at Muni, the PUC, Airport and Port), doubles the term to 10 years, and raises the size of contracts needing Board approval ($10M to $25M).
fiscal: Minimal; possible long-run procurement savings.
pro: Mayor Lurie, SF Democratic Party, SF Chronicle, SPUR, GrowSF, SF Republican Party
con: The League, Tenants Union, Greens

what: Lets the Mayor merge departments (subject to a Board veto), hire and fire most department heads including the police chief, remove most commissioners at will, and appoint deputy mayors again.
fiscal: Minimal; about $250K a year per deputy mayor.
pro: Mayor Lurie, SF Democratic Party, SPUR, GrowSF, Chamber, SF Republican Party
con: DSA, Indivisible SF, Small Business Forward, the League, Tenants Union

t: Weekday cars on the Great Highway
what: Reopens the Upper Great Highway (Lincoln to Sloat) to cars Monday 4am to Friday 6pm; weekends stay park. Partly reverses 2024's Prop K.
fiscal: About $9.8M one-time (mostly signals) plus $0.5–1.9M a year; needs a Coastal Commission permit.
pro: Chinese American Democratic Club, SF Taxpayers Assn, SF Republican Party
con: SF Chronicle, SF Democratic Party, SPUR, GrowSF, Sierra Club, Surfrider

what: A 15-year parcel tax (July 2027–2042) for Muni operations, based on building square footage. $129/yr for a home or condo up to 3,000 sq ft, indexed to inflation. Owner-occupants 65+ exempt.
n: No tax and a larger Muni deficit.
fiscal: About $177M a year from 2027–28. Muni's deficit is about $307M next year.
pro: Mayor Lurie, SF Democratic Party, Chamber, SF Chronicle, SPUR, GrowSF, Tenants Union
con: SF Republican Party (fix SFMTA first), Business League

t: Transfer tax on $10M+ sales to a housing fund
what: For property sales of $10M and up, halves the existing transfer tax and adds an equal 'House SF' tax locked into a housing fund (60% production, 25% acquisition, 10% tenant stabilisation).
y: The money is dedicated to housing.
n: It stays flexible in the general fund.
fiscal: Total revenue barely changes, but about $120M a year moves out of the general fund.
pro: DSA SF, Tenants Union, the League, Affordable Housing Alliance
con: Mayor Lurie, police and fire unions, SF Democratic Party, SPUR, GrowSF, SF Republican Party

what: Removes the transfer-tax exemption on foreclosures of commercial property, hotels and residential buildings of 5+ units. Homes, condos and buildings under 5 units stay exempt.
fiscal: About $100–150M a year on average for 5 years, very volatile.
pro: Mayor Lurie, SF Democratic Party, SEIU 1021, SPUR, GrowSF, Tenants Union
con: SF Taxpayers Assn, SF Republican Party

t: Regional transit sales tax (Connect Bay Area)
type: Regional citizen initiative · majority across 5 counties
what: A 14-year sales tax for BART, Muni, Caltrain, AC Transit and ferries: 1% in SF (the extra half-cent goes to Muni), 0.5% in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo and Santa Clara. About $1B a year region-wide.
n: No tax; transit agencies' cut plans proceed.
fiscal: About $980M–$1B a year region-wide; SF's share mostly to Muni (63%) and BART (29%).
pro: Mayor Lurie, Sen. Wiener, Rep. Pelosi, SF Democratic Party, SF Chronicle, SPUR, GrowSF
con: SF Republican Party (SF pays double), SF Taxpayers Assn, Quentin Kopp
